title: A voice becomes words.
intro: Imagine a tiny team on your laptop. One helper listens, one understands, and one puts the words where you are typing.
story: When you press a shortcut, VOCO listens to your microphone, turns the sound into words, and puts those words at your cursor.
Each part does one job. They pass small messages to each other instead of waiting for one enormous recording.
In this chapter, follow the whole journey. Later chapters open each box and show the real code inside.

steps.label: Shortcut
steps.detail: You press Alt+D. VOCO checks that it is safe to start.

steps.label: Microphone
steps.detail: The microphone turns changing air pressure into a stream of numbers.

steps.label: Speech model
steps.detail: A local trained model predicts words from those numbers.

steps.label: Delivery
steps.detail: VOCO checks the destination and sends the new text.

steps.label: Your cursor
steps.detail: The receiving app accepts the paste. VOCO never presses Enter for you.

facts.title: A team, not one magic function
facts.text: React manages the visible app and recording flow. Rust handles operating-system work. A Python worker calls the native speech library. The receiving app is a separate program.

facts.title: The current route
facts.text: VOCO 2026.0.42 uses NVIDIA Nemotron English 0.6B Q8 on the CPU. Names containing benchmark in the streaming code are historical; they do real production work.

facts.title: Keep the boundary clear
facts.text: The speech worker can return words even if another application refuses a paste. Recognition success and successful delivery are different things.

files.why: Connects the interface, saved preferences and dictation hook.
Coordinates one recording from Start through Stop.
Starts the selected local speech worker.

caution: This guide describes a pinned development source snapshot recorded in its catalog. It does not promise every Linux app or compositor accepts delivery.

quiz.question: Which part owns the text box you are dictating into?
quiz.why: The receiving application owns its own text field. VOCO must respect that boundary.

title: Meet the languages.
intro: Different tools do different jobs, like cooks, waiters and a kitchen manager.
story: TypeScript helps us describe what kind of information is allowed. React uses it to build the interface.
Rust is the careful manager at the door to Linux. Python connects the speech pieces. A compiled native library does the heavy model work.
A language is not a performance score. Where the time goes matters more than the name of the language.

steps.label: TypeScript
steps.detail: Describes data shapes and catches many mistakes before the app runs.

steps.label: React
steps.detail: Updates controls and status when application state changes.

steps.label: Rust
steps.detail: Owns native commands, processes, files and input checks.

steps.label: Python
steps.detail: Validates streaming messages and calls the speech adapter.

steps.label: Native library
steps.detail: Runs trained model calculations using CPU threads.

facts.title: Two kinds of checking
facts.text: TypeScript types disappear when compiled. Rust and Python must still validate messages received at runtime. A correctly typed sender is not a security guarantee.

facts.title: What Tauri provides
facts.text: Tauri connects a WebKit-rendered interface to native Rust commands. An invoke call crosses that boundary; it is not an ordinary same-language function call.

facts.title: How to read unfamiliar syntax
facts.text: An import brings in another tool. A function names a job. A class or struct groups related information. A test checks what happens in a particular situation.

files.why: Typed frontend wrappers for native commands.
Registers native commands and initializes the desktop application.

Lists Rust dependencies.

quiz.question: Does a TypeScript type remove the need to validate a native message?
quiz.why: Runtime messages still need validation at each trust boundary.

title: One press, one recording.
intro: A shortcut is a doorbell. One ring should produce one response, even when two helpers hear it.
story: Linux can report a key press through different routes. VOCO must avoid treating one press as two separate instructions.
During a recording, the shortcut belongs to that recording session. An old callback must not stop a newer session.
If a shortcut has already been consumed, ignoring its callback can lose the user’s only signal. That is why the arbitration rules are careful.

steps.label: Key chord
steps.detail: The configured chord is pressed.

steps.label: Arbitration
steps.detail: VOCO checks which shortcut route currently has authority.

steps.label: Debounce
steps.detail: A repeated observation of the same press is suppressed when appropriate.

steps.label: Session lease
steps.detail: One recording gets a specific ownership token.

steps.label: Release
steps.detail: Finish, cancellation or expiry releases that ownership.

facts.title: Root and focused-window grabs
facts.text: On X11, a passive grab can be attached to the root window or the exact input-focus window. The selected recording scope avoids the root-grab focus disturbance found in testing.

facts.title: IBus is a shortcut helper
facts.text: Protocol 6 does not authorize generic text mutation. It helps deliver the recording trigger; it is not the normal text insertion engine.

facts.title: A lease has an end
facts.text: The X11 recording lease has a fixed 650-second expiry. This covers the 600-second capture limit plus finishing allowance; it is not permission to record forever.

files.why: Receives shortcut events in the interface.
Owns the UUID and renderer epoch for one recording.
Decides which trigger observations may proceed.

caution: An IBus poll in flight is different from completed IBus ownership. Treating them as identical previously lost valid X11 callbacks.

quiz.question: An old recording finishes after a new one starts. What should its callback do?
quiz.why: Session tokens prevent old asynchronous work from changing a replacement recording.

title: Sound becomes numbers.
intro: A microphone makes a very fast flipbook of sound. Each tiny measurement is called a sample.
story: Imagine writing down the height of a wave many times each second. The list of heights is digital audio.
Sample rate means how many measurements happen in one second. It must travel with the numbers, like units on a ruler.
The .43 candidate uses native audio capture on Wayland so the panel can stay hidden. X11 uses WebKit and an AudioWorklet to collect ordered pieces while the interface does other work.

steps.label: Permission
steps.detail: On Wayland, explicitly allow the selected source for this app session. On X11, use browser microphone permission.

steps.label: Device
steps.detail: Bind the recording to the selected input. Native system-default selection resolves to a specific source.

steps.label: Samples
steps.detail: Capture ordered blocks and retain their sample rate through conversion.

steps.label: Descriptor
steps.detail: Keep source, rate and sample-count information together.

steps.label: Queue
steps.detail: Offer the blocks to the recording’s speech queue.

facts.title: A sample is not a word
facts.text: One number says something about the waveform at one instant. Recognition needs patterns across many samples to infer speech.

facts.title: Never guess the rate
facts.text: Calling 44,100 samples “one second at 16 kHz” changes the meaning of the audio. Rate validation and resampling must be deliberate.

facts.title: Permission is not a recording
facts.text: Selecting and allowing a native source does not open a recording. Start begins capture; Stop closes it. A removed source cannot silently become a different microphone.

files.why: Opens and checks browser microphone input.
Retains bounded audio for a recording.
Keeps audio identity and rate facts together.
Handles explicit sample-rate conversion.
Native source selection, permission and bounded capture commands.

caution: The waveform below is a teaching drawing. It never activates your microphone.

quiz.question: What must accompany a list of audio samples?
quiz.why: The rate tells the receiver how much time those samples represent.

title: Audio on a conveyor belt.
intro: Small boxes arrive in order. The next worker opens them one at a time.
story: A queue is a waiting line for work. It lets microphone capture continue while an earlier request is being processed.
Each box carries a session and sequence number. Those labels stop a late reply from being mistaken for the next box.
A bounded queue has a maximum size. If the worker falls too far behind, keeping unlimited audio would make memory and delay grow.

steps.label: Capture
steps.detail: A new ordered block of audio arrives.

steps.label: Label
steps.detail: Attach session, sequence and sample-range metadata.

steps.label: Wait
steps.detail: The block waits behind earlier work.

steps.label: Exchange
steps.detail: Rust sends it to the worker and checks the reply.

steps.label: Account
steps.detail: Update capture, enqueue and response counters.

facts.title: The real bound
facts.text: The production phrase queue rejects backlog beyond three seconds of queued audio. That is a failure boundary, not a desired steady delay.

facts.title: Words have a queue too
facts.text: A newer append-only hypothesis can replace pending output. Text already sent to an external app cannot be blindly replaced or replayed.

facts.title: Counters explain missing work
facts.text: Captured, enqueued and responded samples should reconcile at the queue boundary. Those counts do not prove that a physical microphone captured every spoken sound.

files.why: Serializes the production NVIDIA stream and delivery accounting.
Handles the live phrase-delivery contract.
Supervises bounded worker requests and replies.

caution: The boxes in this simulator are illustrative. They are not measured audio or the real app’s queue.

quiz.question: Why is an unlimited queue a bad idea?
answers: Memory and waiting time could grow without a bound
quiz.why: Limits turn overload into an explicit recoverable problem instead of silent unlimited growth.

title: The speech worker has a rulebook.
intro: Two helpers pass numbered notes through a pipe. Both must agree on what each note means.
story: The Rust backend runs one local Python worker. It sends a line of JSON for each request.
The worker accepts start, push, finish and cancel. It checks the shape and identity of the message before using it.
Normal protocol output is kept separate from native-library diagnostic output, so a log line cannot masquerade as a reply.

steps.label: Start
steps.detail: Open a new recognition stream and remember its session.

steps.label: Push
steps.detail: Add a validated audio block in increasing sequence order.

steps.label: Reply
steps.detail: Return matching session/sequence fields and any new text.

steps.label: Finish
steps.detail: Drain the live stream and return the final hypothesis.

steps.label: Cancel
steps.detail: Close the correct stream without replaying old audio.

facts.title: Small enough to trust
facts.text: worker_main.py bounds each input line to 4 MiB and requires a newline. StreamingSession accepts one-dimensional finite audio blocks no longer than one second at the supplied rate.

facts.title: Numbers are checked too
facts.text: The accepted sample-rate range is 8,000–96,000 Hz, with no rate change inside a session. NaN and infinity are rejected.

facts.title: A stale cancel is special
facts.text: A cancel for a different session is acknowledged without cancelling the active recording. Safety sometimes means intentionally doing nothing.

files.why: Separates protocol stdout before importing the runtime.
Parses, validates and routes protocol messages.
Validates audio and owns each streaming session.
Starts the process, bounds I/O and verifies replies.

caution: A worker that dies during push/finish is not silently restarted with replayed text. Recovery needs a safe session boundary.

quiz.question: Why do replies repeat the session and sequence?
answers: To prove which request they belong to
quiz.why: A correct-looking reply for the wrong recording must still be rejected.

title: How the model guesses words.
intro: The model is a practiced pattern-finder, not a little person reading your mind.
story: Training happened before you installed VOCO. It produced many learned numbers called weights.
During dictation, the model uses those weights and recent audio context to predict text. A runtime is the engine that performs the calculations.
VOCO’s selected model is English-focused. It does not promise automatic language switching.

steps.label: Weights
steps.detail: Load the pinned Q8 model and verify its SHA-256.

steps.label: Recognizer
steps.detail: Create one reusable native recognizer.

steps.label: Stream
steps.detail: Open a stream for this recording.

steps.label: Context
steps.detail: Use incoming audio and recent context to produce hypotheses.

steps.label: Result
steps.detail: Read and free each native result handle.

facts.title: Model versus runtime
facts.text: A model is the learned data; the runtime is the software that executes it. The same model may behave differently with different quantization, threading or streaming settings.

facts.title: The selected configuration
facts.text: The worker defaults to Nemotron English 0.6B Q8, context 1, four CPU threads and the pool backend. Q8 is quantization: a compact representation of model values, not a statement of 98% accuracy.

facts.title: Python is the bridge
facts.text: The Nemotron adapter uses ctypes to call the packaged native library. It defines argument/result types and closes recognizer, stream and result handles to avoid resource leaks.

files.why: Nemotron owns native recognizer and result handles.
Loads and warms the selected configuration.
Reports sanitized runtime identity and readiness.
Records notices for bundled model and library components.

caution: The native binary and model weights are separately provisioned artifacts. Research adapters such as Moonshine are not selectable product features.

quiz.question: What is the difference between model and runtime?
answers: Weights versus the engine that executes them
They are always the same file
quiz.why: The runtime executes calculations using the learned model weights.

title: Words meet the cursor.
intro: Delivering a letter means checking the address, not just finishing the letter.
story: The recognizer’s words travel back to VOCO. Delivery checks whether the intended destination still looks valid.
The normal desktop route uses clipboard replacement and a paste gesture appropriate to the target category.
A successful key command is not proof that an application displayed the words. Some fields offer readback; some do not.

steps.label: Hypothesis
steps.detail: Accept a new append-only text suffix.

steps.label: Destination
steps.detail: Check current focus and available target identity.

steps.label: Clipboard
steps.detail: Place the new text on the clipboard.

steps.label: Paste
steps.detail: Dispatch the appropriate key gesture without Enter.

steps.label: Observe
steps.detail: Use bounded field readback when available.

facts.title: Why spacing needs care
facts.text: Address bars and editors may treat leading spaces specially. The implementation has explicit joining rules and a literal-space path for the legacy helper.

facts.title: Terminals are different
facts.text: Known terminal targets use their paste chord. VOCO does not edit the terminal’s shortcut configuration to make that work.

facts.title: Observation has limits
facts.text: Accessible-field samples are best-effort local observations, not atomic ownership or compositor paint. A target can still change between checks.

files.why: Owns destination checks, clipboard writes and key dispatch.
Collects bounded focus/target identity.
Provides desktop target observations.
Coordinates delivery outcomes in the frontend.

caution: Clipboard paste replaces the current clipboard text. VOCO never automatically sends the message by pressing Enter.

quiz.question: The model returned words but focus changed. What is safer?
answers: Paste into whatever is focused now
quiz.why: Uncertain delivery must not become a blind paste into a different app.

title: Stop means finish the work.
intro: Closing a shop means serving the people already in line before locking the door.
story: Stopping capture and finishing recognition are two different jobs. Some sound can still be waiting in the last capture block.
VOCO drains that tail into the same live stream, asks the model to finish, then waits for remaining delivery.
Only then should the session become idle. Cancellation follows a different path and must not deliver old pending work.

steps.label: Stop capture
steps.detail: Stop accepting new microphone input.

steps.label: Drain tail
steps.detail: Take the final captured samples that have not been offered yet.

steps.label: Finish stream
steps.detail: Finish the existing recognizer stream once.

steps.label: Flush text
steps.detail: Deliver the remaining accepted suffix safely.

steps.label: Idle
steps.detail: Release session ownership and report completion.

facts.title: Do not send the whole recording again
facts.text: The production Stop path forwards retained samples not yet offered. Replaying the whole recording would waste work and could duplicate delivered words.

facts.title: One recording owns its tail
facts.text: Asynchronous guards keep delayed stop/capture callbacks attached to their original recording.

facts.title: Why several timings exist
facts.text: Stop-to-final measures recognition completion. Stop-to-idle includes the rest of shutdown and delivery. Neither is the same as the instant the receiving app paints text.

files.why: Orders the complete Stop sequence.
Waits for final capture blocks.
Coordinates finalization outcomes.
Prevents stale asynchronous updates.
Flushes gated samples and finishes the native stream.

caution: A fast Stop that silently loses the final syllable is a failure, not an optimization.

quiz.question: What should happen to unoffered tail samples at Stop?
answers: Send them into the existing stream
quiz.why: Finish the same stream with only the remaining samples.

title: When something goes wrong.
intro: A good helper says “I’m not sure” instead of pretending the job is done.
story: A microphone can disappear, a worker can stop, a window can change, or a paste can be uncertain.

VOCO keeps recovery explicit. Retry transcribes retained normal-dictation audio with the bundled NVIDIA model, then offers the result for review and Copy. It does not paste it into another application.
Retained audio or text belongs to the recording that produced it. An old error must not overwrite a new session’s state.

steps.label: Notice
steps.detail: Detect capture, worker or delivery failure.

steps.label: Identify
steps.detail: Keep the failed work attached to its session.

steps.label: Retain
steps.detail: Preserve available recovery material.

steps.label: Explain
steps.detail: Show a useful recovery state instead of false success.

steps.label: Retry safely
steps.detail: Recover locally, review the result and copy deliberately.

facts.title: Idle worker repair
facts.text: A confirmed-dead idle worker may be replaced at a safe boundary. That permission does not extend to automatically replaying an in-flight push or finish.

facts.title: State is a map
facts.text: States such as idle, starting, recording and processing make allowed transitions visible. They are more reliable than several unrelated booleans.

facts.title: A separate recovery worker
facts.text: Recovery preserves the original sample rate and uses a bounded private worker. Cancel retains the audio, suppresses late results and cleans up that session; it cannot cancel a newer recovery or live dictation.

files.why: Represents retained recovery work.
Keeps recording identity and lifecycle facts.
Runs explicit offline recovery without a destination callback.
Reaps failed workers and controls restart boundaries.

caution: This guide’s recovery simulator does not kill or restart the installed app.

quiz.question: Why avoid an automatic paste retry after an uncertain result?
answers: It may duplicate or misdirect text
quiz.why: The first paste may already have succeeded. Uncertainty must be handled explicitly.

title: A small interface, clear ownership.
intro: The control panel is the dashboard light, not the engine.
story: The interface shows microphone, shortcut, readiness and recovery. It does not perform neural-network calculations.
A store keeps visible state and preferences together. Native code still owns operating-system authority.
VOCO keeps the normal output fixed to live cursor delivery. Removed assistant and appearance controls are not hidden extra modes.

steps.detail: Update the interface without losing unrelated state.

facts.title: A migration is deliberate
facts.text: The config loader ignores retired fields and fixes cursor output, stable streaming and enhancement off. It preserves microphone, shortcut and onboarding state.

facts.title: Accessibility is part of the design
facts.text: Reduced motion, contrast and transparency follow system preferences. Rounded controls and the silver microphone remain the visual identity.

facts.title: Window movement is native work
facts.text: Dragging/resizing a Tauri window uses native APIs. CSS alone cannot move a Linux desktop window.

quiz.question: Where should Linux input authority live?
answers: In the native backend and its guarded integrations
quiz.why: The UI requests operations; native code enforces their boundaries.

title: One app, several Linux paths.
intro: Linux desktops are neighborhoods with different doorbells and mail slots.
story: X11 and Wayland expose different integration mechanisms. Desktop environments and receiving apps add more variation.
The normal desktop paste route, optional IBus shortcut helper and explicit Chromium field adapter have different contracts.
A test inside one distribution’s container does not test its real default desktop or compositor.

facts.title: Stronger browser identity
facts.text: The explicit browser adapter can check element/document identity, caret and acknowledged prefix. It rejects unsupported fields, including password inputs.

facts.title: Native messaging is local transport
facts.text: The browser host and private socket connect authorized browser work to the desktop. That integration is not a cloud transcription service.

facts.title: A support claim needs the right test
facts.text: Ubuntu userspace, package installation, Hyprland behavior and native microphone operation are separate evidence categories.

quiz.question: Does a successful container test prove the real Hyprland desktop works?
quiz.why: A container shares the host kernel and may not run the target compositor or physical devices.

title: Draw the trust boundaries.
intro: Keep private letters inside the house. Check visitors before opening the door.
story: Normal speech recognition runs locally. It does not require a cloud transcription account.
Local still needs security: files, sockets, child processes, browser messages and clipboard delivery all cross boundaries.
Optional timing logs contain counters and identities, not dictated text or recordings. Update checks contact GitHub.

facts.title: No arbitrary diagnostic strings
facts.text: The worker maps failures to safe error codes rather than logging arbitrary exceptions, request data or transcript text.

facts.title: Private paths must stay private
facts.text: Permissions, symlink checks and same-user socket rules help prevent another local user from redirecting sensitive output.

facts.title: No silent security shortcuts
facts.text: A successful helper command is not proof of safe destination ownership. Content-free logging is not proof that every possible data flow is private.

quiz.question: Which statement is accurate?
answers: Local apps never need security checks
Local apps still need file, process and input boundaries
quiz.why: Local execution reduces some exposures but does not remove local trust boundaries.

title: Measure the right stopwatch.
intro: If two runners start their watches at different times, their numbers cannot be compared fairly.
story: First sound, first hypothesis, first paste dispatch and first observed field update are different moments.
A queue’s waiting time is different from model compute time. Stop-to-idle is different from Stop-to-final.
A measurement needs its clock origin, units, scope and missing evidence. Good charts keep those labels attached.

steps.label: Playback starts
steps.detail: Recorded-audio launch can include leading silence.

steps.detail: An independent observer sees the recipient’s text change.

steps.label: Paint
steps.detail: The compositor draws pixels; this needs separate evidence.

facts.title: Median and p95
facts.text: The median is the middle result. The 95th percentile describes the slow tail of a set of observations. Three repeated recordings are not three different speakers.

facts.title: CPU and memory have scope
facts.text: Worker RSS covers one process. Summed app-tree RSS can count shared memory more than once. CPU-seconds are work consumed, not battery energy.

facts.title: Logs must not become a bottleneck
facts.text: Logging is optional and bounded. Dropped events and missing sequences must be reported because incomplete evidence can make a graph misleading.

files.why: Records frontend/native performance events.

quiz.question: Can helper dispatch time be labeled “pixels appeared”?
quiz.why: The receiver and compositor do additional work. Dispatch is a different observation.

title: Tests are little promises.
intro: A test sets up a situation, performs an action, and checks what should happen.
story: A useful test catches a consequence: a lost final sample, a stale callback, duplicate text or a malformed message.
Unit tests examine small rules. Integration tests exercise cooperating pieces. Native end-to-end tests use real application boundaries.
Passing tests gives evidence for the situations tested. It does not prove every future input will work.

facts.title: Test the failure path
facts.text: A dead worker, a missing microphone or a changed target may reveal defects that a happy-path demonstration misses.

facts.title: Do not erase failed attempts

facts.title: Different proof levels
facts.text: A browser-rendered UI test can mock all native/media boundaries. It proves interface behavior in that harness, not real microphone or desktop insertion.

title: How source becomes an app.
intro: A recipe is not a cake. Building, packaging and checking the result are separate steps.
story: Frontend tools turn TypeScript and CSS into application assets. Rust is compiled into a native executable.
The package must also contain the pinned speech runtime, model artifacts, helper programs and notices.
Checksums and exact identities let us verify which bytes were installed and tested. A matching version label alone is not enough.

facts.title: Lock files are part of the recipe
facts.text: package-lock.json and Cargo.lock pin resolved dependency versions. They are not obsolete copies of the package manifests.

facts.title: A base Tauri package can be incomplete
facts.text: VOCO’s packaging scripts assemble and validate the speech payload. The raw desktop build alone is not the complete distributable.

facts.title: Frozen evidence stays frozen
facts.text: A code change creates new bytes. Tests of an earlier package cannot automatically qualify a newer package, even with the same displayed version.

quiz.question: Is a version string enough to prove two packages are identical?
answers: No; compare exact artifacts and hashes
quiz.why: Different bytes can accidentally share a version label. Artifact identity is stronger.

title: Borrowed code needs care.
intro: You can build a bicycle with borrowed parts, but you still need to know which parts you fitted.
story: A dependency is software that VOCO uses rather than rewriting. Vendored code is a copy kept in the repository.
VOCO vendors glib 0.18.5 with a specific upstream iterator-safety fix. Other GTK/WebKit users must resolve to that same patched copy.
A dependency name on a list is not enough. We need the actual resolved version, patch, license and tests.

facts.title: Why not just add a newer glib?
facts.text: Adding a second glib version can leave GTK using the old vulnerable copy. The fix must reach the library actually used by the dependency graph.

facts.title: Upstream code is a different reading layer
facts.text: The complete catalog includes vendor files. Their implementations belong to their upstream libraries; start with the local patch notes to see VOCO’s changes.

facts.title: No perfect-security badge
facts.text: A fixed issue does not prove that all dependencies have no other risks. Current security documents keep remaining scope separate.

quiz.question: Why can installing a second fixed library version fail to solve an issue?
answers: The application may still use the old copy

title: Open any piece of the code.
intro: Read code like a map: find the entrance, follow the arrows, then inspect one room at a time.
story: Start with the job of a file, not with its first unfamiliar punctuation mark. Read its imports, named functions and tests.
Use the file catalog to find every tracked entry at the pinned commit. Open a file to inspect its exact source and jump to a named symbol.
The chapters explain the central architecture. The catalog supplies complete file coverage; it is not a claim that every upstream line has a hand-written explanation.

facts.title: Production names can mislead
facts.text: benchmarkPhraseQueue.ts and benchmark_stream.rs are live product modules. A historical name is not a reason to delete code.

facts.title: Tests are example stories
facts.text: Find the matching .test.ts or test_*.py file. A well-chosen test often explains a tricky rule more clearly than a long comment.

facts.title: Know what the viewer can show
facts.text: Text blobs up to 2 MB are readable. Binary assets are indexed with size and Git identity. Native binaries and model weights supplied outside Git are explained as external artifacts.

answers: How many lines can I delete?
What job and invariant does this file own?

title: Measure before we optimize.
intro: A quicker transcript is useful only if it keeps your words, meaning and punctuation intact.
story: This chapter teaches the evaluation method used by VOCO contributors. The dated measurements were collected on the .41 development snapshot; the .42 release preserves its model and defaults. These experiments are not fresh .42 performance measurements.

A stopwatch and exact text comparison answer different questions from a language model. Code measures timing, word errors and delivery failures. TypeSafe judges whether a transcript preserves meaning.

We give Jev a public reference and a transcript, plus separate questions for meaning and consequential mistakes. Punctuation judgments need an audited reference. Personal dictation never enters this research service; VOCO itself remains local.

We challenge the judge before trusting it, freeze the speech fixtures, then run the same audio through baseline and candidate settings. We keep unsuccessful experiments because they explain why a tempting change was rejected.

steps.label: Define
steps.detail: Freeze timing boundaries, reference text, rubric and rejection rules before measuring.

steps.label: Measure
steps.detail: Replay the same public audio and record timings, word errors and resources.

steps.label: Judge
steps.detail: Ask TypeSafe narrow questions about meaning; retain probabilities and uncertainty.

steps.label: Compare
steps.detail: Compare repeated trials and separate speakers. Missing evidence stays missing.

steps.label: Decide
steps.detail: Reject regressions. A higher average never excuses a wrong destination or lost meaning.

facts.title: What contributors provide
facts.text: Evidence, explicit question criteria, a model version, an API key for live evaluation and independently labeled cases. The skill does not award a built-in app grade.

facts.title: What a score means
facts.text: Meaning has four concrete levels: contradicted or absent; an important detail wrong; only a minor detail lost; all meaning preserved. A score divided by three and multiplied by 100 is a rubric position, not word accuracy. Confidence is not a truth guarantee.

facts.title: Check the judge too
facts.text: The 16 authored challenge cases produced 10 true material-error flags and six true negatives at a provisional 0.5 threshold. This small synthetic check is not independent human calibration. An invented action still received 2.10/3 for overall meaning, so the separate consequential-error question matters.

facts.title: The measurements still missing
facts.text: These public audiobook references have no audited punctuation or word-end times. We cannot honestly score punctuation accuracy, word-end-to-screen latency, physical microphone quality or worldwide rank from them.

facts.title: Where to reproduce it
facts.text: Follow docs/testing/typesafe-evaluation.md. Provision the pinned runtime, use public fixtures, freeze the rubric and reference text, then run the local measurement and optional TypeSafe tools. Keep API keys and raw receipts out of Git.

files.why: Measures the real pinned worker with public audio fixtures.
Asks narrow semantic questions only after explicit opt-in.
Defines metric boundaries, targets and reproducible commands.

caution: The comparison is an experiment, not a world ranking or a release. Worker output, observed recipient text and painted pixels are different boundaries. No production setting changes automatically from a TypeSafe score.

quiz.question: A candidate has a higher meaning score but inserts text into the wrong window. What happens?
answers: Accept it because its average improved
Reject it: delivery safety is a separate hard gate
Ask the model to average the two
quiz.why: Safety failures cannot be compensated by better speed or a higher semantic score.

comparison.title: 19 September 2026 · same .41 runtime and model
comparison.scope: 24 paired real-time worker trials across 12 public-fixture speakers. A–B–B–A run order. TypeSafe judged one transcript per speaker and setting; repeated playback does not add independent speakers. Four isolated packaged GTK/X11 trials use one public clip, two trials per setting; their ranges are descriptive and state observation polls every 50 ms.
rows: Worker first text from paced replay, median
Private GTK: Start command → active observation
Private GTK: playback launch → first field text
Private GTK: Stop command → idle observation
comparison.decision: Decision: retain the current context 1 setting. Context 0 improves one development recognition error but uses about 49% more service time, barely changes first-text timing and does not improve held-out accuracy or meaning.
comparison.limits: Experimental results, not a shipped before/after improvement or worldwide ranking. Word timestamps and punctuation gold are absent. These worker numbers are not shortcut, recipient or pixel-paint timings. TypeSafe scores are rubric positions, not percentages of correct words.

additional.title: Same context 1 · CPU-thread follow-up
rows: Median first hypothesis from paced replay
additional.scope: 24 trials per setting across the same 12 public fixtures. The six-thread runs followed the earlier baseline; this follow-up was not counterbalanced in time.
additional.decision: Promising local compute headroom: 11.2% less median service time on the AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 8840HS test system, with only 4.6 ms earlier first text. Retain the portable four-thread default until loaded-desktop, energy and other-CPU checks support a change.
additional.limits: This is not a shipped speedup or a six-thread desktop qualification. Complete text parity allows reuse of existing semantic judgments; no extra TypeSafe calls or new independent speakers are implied.

sourceNote: Evaluation tools from the pinned 2026.0.43 development snapshot. Tables retain their original .41 experiment identity.

title: One VOCO, different Linux desktops.
intro: A download is ready only when installation, microphone, shortcut and text delivery work together.
story: VOCO keeps a shared recognition model and application source. Native Debian, Fedora, openSUSE and Arch packages translate that application into dependencies each system understands.
The desktop matters too. A package can install correctly while a compositor handles windows, shortcuts or clipboard access differently. Omarchy needs Hyprland testing as well as Arch package testing.
The .43 work is a development candidate. Public .42 remains the released Debian package. The support plan records what is measured and what still blocks each additional package.

steps.label: Package
steps.detail: Resolve native dependencies and verify every installed payload file.

steps.label: Desktop
steps.detail: Run the intended compositor in a booted guest and finish fresh-user setup.

steps.label: Dictation
steps.detail: Send public fixture audio, observe the receiving field and check Start and Stop.

steps.label: Failures
steps.detail: Switch focus, repeat sessions, interrupt devices and retain recovery safely.

steps.label: Release
steps.detail: Sign exact qualified artifacts and verify the downloaded copies before installation.

facts.title: Before: a transparent tile
facts.text: Hyprland kept the off-screen VOCO window tiled. An isolated test reproduced it even though short dictation worked.

facts.title: Why hiding alone failed
facts.text: A diagnostic native hide removed the tile, but a fresh WebKit microphone request did not become active within 25 seconds. That failed attempt led to native capture qualification.

facts.title: After: native capture while hidden
facts.text: The installed .43 Arch candidate passed fresh setup under Omarchy’s packaged desktop configuration: 14 normalized words, a truly hidden panel, an unchanged second field and a 244 ms Stop. A 577.68-second repetition delivered 1,162 normalized words and passed independent full-audio checks. These individual VM observations do not certify physical microphones or arbitrary apps.

facts.title: A measured shortcut improvement
facts.text: The candidate's voco --toggle command used a compositor binding without keyboard-device access. One isolated fixture delivered all 14 words and left the second field unchanged. This does not certify every shortcut or application.

facts.title: Fit the available CPUs
facts.text: A two-core VM took 35.37 seconds to warm a four-thread recognizer, exceeding startup limits. Two threads took 1.53 seconds in a controlled check. The candidate caps its default at the available CPUs, up to four. All 12 public fixtures produced identical transcripts across the tested Fedora, openSUSE and two-core Ubuntu workers: six lexical edits in 238 words. This small corpus does not establish worldwide accuracy.

facts.title: Reject an unknown destination
facts.text: An X11 focus-switch test caught text continuing into a second field. GNOME exposed both the client and its decoration as active, and VOCO incorrectly allowed an unbound paste. The candidate distinguishes the decoration and requires a destination token. The installed regression then left the second field empty and retained recovery. Successful ordinary dictation had not exposed this bug.

facts.title: Let desktop focus settle safely
facts.text: A fresh Fedora GNOME setup queued about 970 accessibility events after hiding the panel. The old 256-event budget rejected Start. The candidate drains ordinary transition backlogs within a 50 ms time limit, while still refusing an unsettled destination. Installed Fedora GNOME and openSUSE KDE tests then passed repeated dictation, focus departure and explicit recovery after source loss.

facts.title: Test the receiving application
facts.text: Kate and Konsole accepted the public fixture in a booted KDE guest. Firefox exposed both shortcut-modifier interference and CPU contention that GTK-only tests had missed. Two controlled trials passed with an unused F8 compositor binding and one recognizer thread on two CPUs, but Stop took 2.0 and 3.0 seconds. The next candidate leaves one CPU available for desktop work, capped at four recognizer threads, and needs fresh package qualification. These controls are evidence, not a universal speed claim.

facts.title: Safe upgrades
facts.text: Debian preserves existing directory modes during upgrades. A real legacy-install test exposed inherited group-write permissions. A narrowly checked migration repairs only the known package-owned mode, preserving custom permissions and personal settings.

facts.title: Keep obligations installed
facts.text: RPM can omit ordinary documentation on minimal systems. License files need explicit license metadata so those terms remain installed.

facts.title: What TypeSafe contributes
facts.text: Optional semantic judgments assess a transcript's meaning. Exact code and real desktop tests establish package identity, audio timing, destination safety and compatibility. A language-model score cannot replace those checks.

files.why: The support scope, setup and remaining release gates.
Explicit native dependency profiles and license metadata.
Private, single-attempt compositor control transport.
Dated outcomes and qualification limits.

caution: These are development experiments, not a released universal Linux installer. The Omarchy long-session result uses virtual audio and one GTK recipient. Fedora GNOME and openSUSE KDE also have installed virtual-audio trials. Physical microphones and the wider application matrix still need their own evidence.

quiz.question: The RPM installs, but dictation fails under the default compositor. Is that distribution ready?
answers: No: package and desktop acceptance are separate gates
quiz.why: A native package is only one part of the experience. The microphone, shortcut, window and destination must work together.
